newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief to set up new massacre probe for Congo.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief to set up new massacre probe for Congo.

text.p: The United Nations said on Monday Secretary-General Kofi Annan would organise a new mission to probe massacres in the former Zaire, a move human rights groups say gives in to President Laurent Kabila's objections to the original Geneva-based mission.
"The secretary-general feels it is not who does this report but that it be done," U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said, adding that Annan would inform the Security Council of its intention on Tuesday.
"I don't think it has ever been done that an investigatory human rights mission has been launched by the secretary-general," Eckhard added.
At stake is a pariah status for the Democratic Republic of the Congo and much needed aid Kabila is seeking if a U.N. mission is not given free rein to pursue its probe, diplomats said.

The government of Congo, formerly Zaire, has blocked an investigation of reported massacre sites in the eastern part of the country, demanding that the team leader be replaced and its tasks redefined. Rebel troops loyal to Kabila are accused of killing Rwandan Hutu refugees during their push across eastern Zaire last year.

Numerous envoys said both Annan and U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson, when they met Kabila last month to urge he allow an investigation, tacitly agreed to his demand that Roberto Garreton of Chile, the special investigator in the former Zaire, be excluded from any mission.

Kabila also wants the probe to cover the years before rebels loyal to him and Rwandan troops were engaged against the refugees, a demand that may be easier to fulfil. But he has also put restrictions on the movement of the team, which the United Nations has difficulty in accepting.
Garreton visited the country briefly in March and concluded that there was enough evidence to warrant a full investigation of massacres.
He had a list of about 40 sites given to him by eyewitnesses but Kabila contends Garreton came to conclusions before he was able to actually conduct a probe.

Felice Gaer of the Jacob Blaustein Institute and a sometimes U.S. delegate to the Geneva-based U.N. Human Rights Commission, said: "The United States has always been the strongest supporter of the integrity of the human rights commission and the independence of its investigators."

She noted that Washington refused to back down when Sudan refused a U.N. rapporteur or investigator until they let him in. They have also insisted Cuba allow a rapporteur chosen by the commission. "I can't understand this," she said.

On the other hand, Gaer said it was important to get into Zaire quickly and if the Security COuncil authorised the trip it would give it status that would be hard for Kabila to refuse without a public showdown.

"But don't assume the mission is going to stop the massacres without putting pressure on where the pressure belongs -- which is on the government of Rwanda, which is in control of the troops, and by Kabila asserting his authority as the true president of the whole country," she said.
Kenneth Roth, director of Human Rights Watch said: "Garreton is not accused of reporting inaccurately but of reporting too early."
"He is being penalised of trying to play a preventive role, of reporting in an effort to stop the killings," he said. "Richardson just didn't think through the consequences."
